title: Combinations (nCr)
tagline: Year 3 — Selections, committees, geometry counts, distribution of objects and restrictions

introduction.overview: A combination is a selection in which order does not matter. Choosing r objects from n different objects can be done in nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!) ways. Combinations count committees, teams, hands of cards, diagonals and triangles in geometry, and distributions of objects into groups. They connect directly to permutations: nPr = nCr × r!.
introduction.placementRelevance: Combination questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually with committees under conditions, geometry counts and distributions.
introduction.realWorldContext: Choosing project teams, lottery tickets and test subsets are combinations.

learningObjectives: Use nCr and its symmetry nCr = nC(n − r)
Form committees with conditions (at least, at most, specific members)

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: nCr = nPr / r!. nC0 = nCn = 1. nCr = nC(n − r).

coreDefinitions: nCr: the number of ways to choose r objects from n distinct objects, order ignored.
Selections with conditions: use "at least" as complement or by cases.
Distribution into labelled groups: choose for the first, then the second, and so on; divide by repeats for identical groups.
Geometry counts: choose points and apply conditions (no three collinear etc.).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A selection ignores order, so each selection is counted r! times if you count arrangements. Dividing by r! corrects the overcounting. For conditions, count by cases or subtract the unwanted selections from the total.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Decide whether order matters. If not, use nCr. For "at least one", subtract "none" from the total. For specific people, include or exclude them first.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Geometry
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Lines = nC2;  Triangles = nC3 (no three collinear);  Diagonals = nC2 − n

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Groups
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Divide by k! for k identical groups of equal size

mainNarrative: Use nCr when order does not matter. From 8 students choose a team of 3: 8C3 = 8 × 7 × 6 / 6 = 56. By symmetry 10C8 = 10C2 = 45.
For committees with conditions, work by cases or complements. A committee of 3 is chosen from 4 men and 3 women with at least one woman: total 7C3 = 35 minus all-men 4C3 = 4 gives 31.

For specific members, include or exclude them first. A committee of 4 from 8 people that includes two particular people: choose the other 2 from the remaining 6: 6C2 = 15; that excludes both: 6C4 = 15.
Geometry counts are combinations of points. Lines from 6 points, no three collinear, number 6C2 = 15. Triangles: 6C3 = 20. Diagonals of an n-gon: nC2 − n; for a hexagon 15 − 6 = 9.
For distributions, divide by the factorial of the number of identical groups. Dividing 6 different people into 3 pairs gives 6!/(2!³ × 3!) = 15 (the 3! removes the order of the groups).

deepDiveAspects.title: Combine selection and arrangement
deepDiveAspects.content: Select first, then arrange: choosing 3 from 8 and arranging them gives 8C3 × 3! = 336 = 8P3.

deepDiveAspects.title: Pascal's identity
deepDiveAspects.content: nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr is a quick way to check or simplify sums of combinations.

solvedExamples.title: At least one
solvedExamples.question: A committee of 3 is chosen from 4 men and 3 women. In how many ways can it contain at least one woman?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The complement is easier to count.

solvedExamples.title: Geometry
solvedExamples.question: How many diagonals does a hexagon have?

solvedExamples.title: Groups
solvedExamples.question: In how many ways can 6 different people be divided into 3 pairs?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Divide by the order of the pairs.

shortcutMethods.title: Cases or complement

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Use nCr; for "at least" subtract the complement; for specific people include or exclude them first; for identical groups divide by k!.

rulesForApplication: Divide by k! for equal groups.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Choosing one woman then the rest freely.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: nCr is always an integer and at most (n choose n/2); reject options outside.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Use symmetry to reduce the arithmetic.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I handle at least one?
